title: Meta Andromeda: Powering the Next Generation of Ads Retrieval Through Model-System Co-Design
abstract: This post describes the next generation of Meta Andromeda, Meta’s personalized ads retrieval engine, and how co-designing the model, system, and GPU hardware unlocks a new efficiency frontier for ads retrieval. In production, the system scores every eligible ad with near ranking-level model performance at retrieval scale and surfaces the top candidates at over one billion ads per second, a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models (i.e., a 100x lift compared to the 2024 Meta Andromeda system). For advertisers, this means better performance automatically from the retrieval system matching ads across a larger candidate pool, within the same latency budget. Since 2025, Meta Andromeda has delivered a 2.4% increase in conversions on Facebook. Meta Andromeda is Meta’s machine learning system for personalized ads retrieval, the first stage of the ads recommendation pipeline. Retrieval narrows a vast pool of eligible ads down to a small set of strong candidates in milliseconds; a later, more computationally expensive ranking stage then scores those survivors in fine detail. Historically, the deep modeling quality of the ranking stage has been too costly to apply at retrieval’s scale. Building on the retrieval foundation established with Andromeda’s 2024 launch on the NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip, this post shares how co-designing the model, system, and hardware together brings near ranking-level performance to the retrieval scale. Challenges and Opportunities in Scaling Retrieval The 2024 Andromeda deployment reimplemented retrieval with an end-to-end optimized retrieval implementation from custom AI hardware with hierarchical indexing and GPU-native operators to a purpose-built ML model, growing model capacity by four orders of magnitude. Since then, generative AI creative tools have helped advertisers rapidly create hundreds of millions of new ads, growing Meta’s ads candidate pool to an unprecedented scale. Scoring such a large ad candidate pool with a more accurate model at a much higher system throughput requires fundamental technology breakthroughs in model quality, system architecture, and hardware utilization jointly. Higher Model Performance Requires a New Architecture Ads retrieval has an outsized ROI on incremental quality: Small improvements in retrieval model performance can drive large gains in advertiser value. The rapid expansion of our ads candidate pool makes optimizing for hardware capacity ROI an increasingly critical factor. The 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval models have established a highly effective foundation with their GPU-optimized deep neural network architecture. To keep improving retrieval performance at a sustainable compute cost at our current scale, however, we must move beyond that paradigm. This requires a fundamental architectural evolution to push model performance boundaries significantly without a proportional increase in costs. New System Bottlenecks at Billion Scale The 2024 Meta Andromeda system evaluates at tens of millions of ads per second per GPU card. Meeting the new business demand requires a throughput at multi-billion ads evaluated per second per card in the system. At billions of ads per second throughput, the memory bandwidth of passing ad tensors through memory hierarchy becomes the new bottleneck. Intermediate tensors between GPU kernels account for terabytes per second of memory traffic, and shipping ads between local CPU hosts and remote hardware accelerators evaluating models saturates the network link. This requires a new system co-design that unifies these fragmented, distributed workloads into a single GPU pipeline. Pushing Towards the Hardware Limits With retrieval running on GPU, the important optimization question is “How close are we to the hardware ceiling, and how much room remains for future model growth?” Answering this requires pushing each component of the retrieval pipeline to the limits of the current hardware generation, a challenge that motiva

title: Building an Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: If you’ve tried to get an agent into production, the model and tool use are not the blocker. The main bottleneck is everything around them: how many teams can build within a secure environment, which team owns each model and tool, how AgentOps and error handling stay inside a pre-defined boundary, and how platform, Workstream, and finance teams see cost and health across accounts. For a Platform team that wants to support many agentic use cases, that’s a platform product to design and operate. In this post, we refer to the team that manages the platform as the Platform team, and to the teams that build on it as Workstream teams. Workstream teams are the domain or product teams that build and own agents on the platform. Each Workstream team needs a paved road with approved models and tools, short-lived workload identity, isolated runtime and memory, automated evaluation, rollback, telemetry, and cost attribution. These controls need to remain consistent as Workstream teams customize prompts, tools, data access, and application behavior. When every team assembles them, controls drift, shared services become a bottleneck, and ownership is difficult to audit. In this post, we walk through the architecture and reference implementation of an enterprise Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover the multi-account operating model, the Platform control plane, a repeatable per-Workstream deployment pattern, separate inference and tool gateways, and an evaluation pipeline that gates each agent before promotion to production. By the end, you should be able to deploy a governed Workstream from the companion blueprint, validate its security and lifecycle contracts, and use it as the foundation for your own agentic AI platform in the organization. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides modular services for building, deploying, and operating agents at scale, including runtime, gateway, identity, memory, policy, registry, and evaluations. The Enterprise Agentic AI Platform Blueprint , built on AgentCore, adds the surrounding enterprise contracts as deployable infrastructure as code: ownership, account boundaries, software delivery, observability, cost governance, and retirement. Architectural principles Before diving into the solution details, it helps to understand the organizational needs that drive the platform architecture. The common challenges we have heard from customers who establish an agent platform fall into these five categories: Governed model access: Every untrusted inference request must pass through an approved inference gateway. The gateway applies the organization’s guardrails (for example, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails or a third-party provider), restricts which models and inference AWS Regions each Workstream can use, and enforces per-Workstream rate limits, token quotas, and budgets so that no single team can exhaust shared capacity. It also carries workload identity and emits attribution data. Governed tool access: Agents must discover and invoke only approved tools through an authenticated Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, with exact targets, least-privilege execution roles, policy decisions, and an auditable owner. Delegated delivery: Workstream teams (for example, product teams) need to ship and roll back independently inside pre-approved boundaries, without waiting for the platform team to deploy each application or granting developers a direct infrastructure write path. Fleet operations and cost: Several personas need visibility across accounts without gaining write access to team workloads. Agent operations engineers need logs, metrics, traces, and quotas. Workstream owners need cost per agent against their budgets. FinOps and finance teams need chargeback by team or business unit through AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) . Security and governance leads need evidence of which workload called which model and tool. Bounded evidence and lifecycle: Every agent release

title: Timestral
abstract: We introduce Timestral, a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M and Timestral-123M take the top two places on every metric. We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context. This report describes the model design and its benchmark results. Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face and inference code on GitHub.

title: Distributed training with Ray Train DLCs and EFA on EKS
abstract: What usually stops PyTorch training from scaling out to a cluster is the container, not the model code. Every container needs the same CUDA runtime , a PyTorch build compiled against it, NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library), the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) userspace libraries, the AWS OFI NCCL plugin that connects NCCL to EFA, and a Ray version the cluster operator agrees with. Building that image and rebuilding it each time one of those pieces moves is a project of its own, and it has nothing to do with the model you set out to train. The Ray Train Deep Learning Container (DLC) is that image, built by AWS. AWS assembles the stack, tests it as one unit, publishes it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) Public and keeps it patched. Figure 1: One EKS cluster with a control plane managed by AWS, a CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) running the KubeRay operator and Ray head, and two EFA-enabled g6.12xlarge nodes in one Availability Zone. KubeRay builds it from one RayCluster manifest, Ray Train places eight workers, one per GPU, and inter-node collectives cross over EFA. Ray runs a job across machines as a single cluster with two roles. The Ray head coordinates and runs the global control store that tracks cluster state, the dashboard and job server you submit jobs to. Ray worker nodes supply the GPUs and run the training processes. Each worker joins the cluster by connecting to the head’s address when it starts. On Kubernetes, each of these is a pod. Kubernetes has no built-in idea of a Ray cluster, so something must create the head and worker pods, start Ray in the right role in each, point the workers at the head, and replace pods that fail. KubeRay does this. It’s an open source Kubernetes operator that adds a RayCluster resource: you describe a head group and a worker group in one manifest, and KubeRay builds and maintains the cluster from it. A single tagged image runs as both the Ray head and the Ray workers, whether KubeRay starts it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) or you start it yourself on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2). What you add is configuration: which instances, how many GPUs each pod gets, which network transport NCCL uses, and which extra Python packages a job needs. All of it is set from outside the image. This post walks through a sample that uses the DLC exactly as published to fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B with PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) across eight NVIDIA L4 GPUs on two g6.12xlarge instances. The training code is one function, the cluster is one RayCluster manifest plus a file of variables, and no image is built at any point. Because the DLC already carries the EFA stack, collectives between the two instances run over the EFA as soon as the pods request it. The entire solution is in this sample repository , and it uses the same KubeRay-on-EKS foundation as our multi-node Ray Serve walkthrough . What you get without building anything The Ray Train DLC is the PyTorch training image with Ray’s training libraries on top. title: V-LUMEN: Visual Lookup Memory for Embedding Scaling in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Embedding-level scaling expands the capacity of language models through lookup-based memory rather than by increasing model depth, width, or dense computation. Extending this idea to vision-language models (VLMs) is challenging because visual features are continuous, spatially structured, and query-dependent, unlike discrete text tokens that naturally support n-gram lookup. We introduce V-LUMEN, a visual lookup memory for VLMs. V-LUMEN discretizes visual features with a frozen codebook, builds spatially aware memory keys through spatial aggregation-based hashing, and modulates them with text-conditioned relevance signals; all addressing is non-parametric, and the retrieved embeddings are fused into the backbone through a gated residual pathway. On five reasoning-intensive benchmarks, V-LUMEN substantially improves a frozen Qwen3-VL-2B backbone and transfers zero-shot to three benchmarks whose images are disjoint from the training data. At a matched parameter budget, moving part of a LoRA or MoE adapter's capacity into V-LUMEN preserves accuracy on two backbones, indicating that external visual memory is an independent capacity axis rather than a stronger adaptation method. Because lookup cost is constant in table size and incurred only once at prefill, this capacity grows in storage rather than in per-token compute. Code is available at https://github.com/miso-choi/V-Lumen.

title: Pneuma: A Large-Scale Real-World Time Series Benchmark for Commercial Aircraft Predictive Maintenance
abstract: Predictive maintenance is vital for commercial aviation, yet progress remains hindered by the lack of public, large-scale real-world datasets. As a result, most methods are developed and evaluated on proprietary data, limiting reproducibility. We introduce Pneuma, the first publicly available large-scale benchmark for predictive maintenance using onboard time series from in-service commercial aircraft. Built around bleed air systems, Pneuma contains over 920 million multivariate time steps across four aircraft types and 9 verified fault scenarios, directly aligned with real maintenance logs. The dataset exhibits key real-world challenges, including substantial class imbalance, subtle fault evolution patterns, and significant variance across aircraft configurations. We structure the benchmark around three tasks: multivariate forecasting, supervised fault classification, and unsupervised anomaly detection, with labels derived from actual maintenance records. Under unified settings, we evaluate over 25 models from four methodological families on 9 carefully curated subsets. The results reveal that even strong contemporary models struggle with subtle fault signatures. Further analyses show consistent gains from additional in-context examples and multivariate inference, while forecasting quality is strongly associated with anomaly detection performance. Together, these findings provide practical insights into effectively modeling complex real-world aviation time series. We hope Pneuma will serve as a rigorous and reproducible foundation for advancing data-driven predictive maintenance toward real-world deployment in commercial aviation.

title: Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops
abstract: Relations compose through the entity they share - Alice is Bob's mother and Bob is Carol's father, so Alice is Carol's grandmother - and the order matters, since a father's mother is not a mother's father; verifying a composed relation means closing the loop. We show that if each entity's coordinate frame may be rotated independently (per-entity frame freedom), three things follow. In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact at all. The only gauge-invariant score of a triangle is a class function of its holonomy $H = T_{ij} T_{jk} T_{ki}$ - a Wilson loop. And the only equivariant update of an edge is $U = Ψ(H)\, T_{ij}$ with $Ψ$ conjugation-equivariant. Edge attention by Wilson loops is therefore not one design among many but the unique form the symmetry permits. Three communities hold pieces of this form: the commuting-operator embeddings of knowledge graphs are its abelian (commuting) sector; AlphaFold's triangle update and the Edge Transformer have its shape - an edge updated through the third vertex - without its constraints; and lattice QCD builds it equivariantly on lattices. We instantiate the equivariant sub-family on general relational graphs as holonomy attention. With no training and composition alone, it infers unobserved $S_4$ relations on sparse graphs at 0.88 with a fifth of the edges corrupted, at or slightly below specialist synchronization algorithms, where every commutative architecture is capped at 0.083; its holonomy score flags corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99 where commuting scores are capped at 0.76 by a second selection rule, and it separates clusters without labels.

title: Identifying and disentangling direct and spillover effects using multiple pre-treatment periods
abstract: Under interference, the treatment of some units affects the outcomes of others, so that the effect on a treated unit consists of a direct and a spillover component. A non-treated comparison group then generally identifies neither component, but the difference between the total effect on the treated and the spillover effect on the comparison units. We show that both components are identified separately when multiple pre-treatment periods are available, without an uncontaminated comparison group. Under no anticipation, pre-treatment outcomes are free of both components for every unit. Extrapolating the pre-treatment trend within a group, as in interrupted time series approaches, therefore identifies the counterfactual outcome in the absence of any treatment. Applied to the treated it gives the total effect on them, applied to the non-treated at a given level of exposure the spillover effect on them. Disentangling the two components in addition requires effect homogeneity across treated and non-treated units with the same exposure and covariates, as well as common support in exposure. We derive doubly robust and Neyman-orthogonal expressions for the effects of interest, which permits controlling for covariates by machine learning, and establish asymptotic normality. A simulation study confirms the root-$n$ behaviour of the estimators and the reliability of the standard errors. We apply the framework to the compulsory licensing of enemy-owned patents in the United States in 1919. Licensing raised patenting in the licensed subclasses and in technologically close ones alike, so that a comparison-group design understates the total effect.

title: When uncertainty quantification fails: structural vulnerabilities and corrections for selective prediction under clinical class imbalance
abstract: Background. Selective prediction systems improve the safety of clinical artificial intelligence by deferring ambiguous cases to human experts while automating high-confidence decisions. However, this safety mechanism relies entirely on the premise that uncertainty scores accurately reflect clinical ambiguity. In prognostic tasks characterized by severe class imbalance, where the clinical outcome of interest is a minority, this assumption breaks down. Standard uncertainty measures cease to capture clinically aligned ambiguity; instead, they become a proxy for class membership, systematically penalizing minority patients regardless of their individual predictive clarity. Results. Across 56 synthetic conditions and three neurodegenerative cohorts spanning severe class imbalance to near-balanced conditions (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's Disease, Alzheimer's Disease), our framework consistently maintained bounded, balanced risk across trajectories. In contrast, global metrics either collapsed minority Sensitivity or protected the minority at the expense of majority patients. Applying CCR with standard entropy fails to protect the minority because it breaks within-class monotonicity when tau=0.5. Combining CCR with threshold-aware metrics restores strict monotonicity, correctly identifies ambiguous patients, and safely mitigates minority exclusion. Conclusions. Under clinical class imbalance, standard uncertainty quantification measures dataset sparsity rather than clinical ambiguity, creating a systemic illusion of safety. This bias is a correctable structural flaw. Clinical pipelines deploying selective prediction under imbalance should adopt threshold-aligned uncertainty measures and class-stratified evaluation. This reduces class-specific risk imbalance, supporting safer selective prediction under the evaluated conditions without silently excluding the most vulnerable patients.

title: Meta Models: Models that Model Learning
abstract: Every neural-network training run produces not only a model, but also evidence about how models learn. Can these accumulated experiments enable us to predict and compare new training runs before executing them? We study meta-models: models that predict the learning behavior of other models. From this perspective, final-performance prediction, learning-curve prediction, and hyperparameter selection are different queries to the same training response function. We take a first, humble empirical step toward this goal: treating real language-model training records as native numeric data, we find that an off-the-shelf tabular in-context learner, TabPFN, can match or outperform a fine-tuned LLM meta-model in multiple evaluated settings. Whereas recent work fine-tunes LLMs on tokenized configurations at a cost of tens to hundreds of GPU-hours, TabPFN requires seconds of fit-and-predict time without task-specific weight updates. We argue that meta-modeling is better treated as its own numeric modality rather than as a text task for LLMs. Going one step further, augmenting TabPFN with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) further improves accuracy on selected prediction tasks. Finally, we pre-registered a forecast of the Marin Hero Run, a 535B-parameter public training run, whose ground truth is revealed point by point as training progresses, putting meta-model predictions to the test against training outcomes not yet observed at the time of forecasting.

title: Are You Getting Your Money’s Worth From AI?
abstract: The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. Software development has emerged as the biggest beneficiary of AI automation. One CIO I talked to recently, with 170 people in his organization, measured a 2.1x increase in productivity from AI. That productivity came at a cost. His top users of AI each spent $21,000 on tokens per month. Another engineering leader spends six to eight thousand dollars per engineer per month. This is not a trivial amount of money. Eventually, it has to come from somewhere, and it will probably come from your personnel budget. Now we’re talking about real consequences for real people’s lives. But there are also real business consequences for not acting. If you’re going to make those choices—and somebody is going to—they need to be good ones. So you need to know more than the costs; you need to know the benefits too. Are you getting a good return on your investment in AI? Is there another way of using AI that would be better? How do you know what you’re getting? Anecdotal reports abound, but the reasoning behind those anecdotes are often, to put it politely, not ideal. Some claims are outright fiction. Given the stakes, that’s a problem. In this essay series, I’ll show you how to assess the impact of AI on software development in your organization. It’s in four parts plus an epilogue: Why, and what not to do (this essay) Measuring delivery speed Measuring and modeling unintended consequences Modeling and forecasting business outcomes Epilogue: Notes for your CFO Why you need to quantify impact Engineering leaders everywhere are feeling pressure to do more with AI. But which approach is best? There are a lot of people with strident opinions about what to do, but not a lot of consensus, and even less hard data. Even if there were hard data, it’s not one-size-fits-all. A solution that works best for an internal IT development shop isn’t necessarily the one that works best for a startup, and the approach that’s best for a new product isn’t necessarily the one that’s best for a crafty legacy system. Faster approaches aren’t necessarily better, either. If you get twice as much done per person, but spend so much money on tokens that you have to cut your staff in half, have you actually seen any ROI? You might actually be better off with a more modest speed boost if it keeps your costs down. You can’t make these trade-offs from a gut feeling alone. In a famous METR study , engineers thought AI made them 49% faster than it actually did. 1 You have to measure impact to know what you’re actually getting. Don’t neglect costs Costs are much easier to measure than impact, but they’re not without their own challenges. The biggest one is subsidies. In the fight to gain market share, big AI firms are offering substantial discounts. One engineering leader told me each team member was spending thousands of dollars in tokens at the cost of a $200 subscription. Anthropic and OpenAI are constantly offering discounts and other promotions. At some point, these subsidies will end, and prices will go up. Or will they? Open-weight models and local inference are exerting downward pressure on token costs. Dedicated inference chips could make tokens cheaper. Routers promise to direct your prompts to the cheapest model for the job. Models could require fewer tokens to accomplish the same task as they become more capable. All of these factors could actually cause prices to go down. When you calculate ROI, don’t assume today’s costs are the ones you should model. Whether you think prices will go up, down, or remain the same, make your assumptions explicit, and consider modeling both optimistic and pessimistic scenarios. One more wrinkle: Adopting AI isn’t a matter of flipping a switch. People will need time to learn how to apply it. As with any big shift, change management isn’t to be underestimated.
